title: Mountains of prey and the overthrow of the proud
english: So he calls the mountains of the land flowing with milk and honey mountains of prey and food, from which he says God will be seen in a manner surpassing all greatness. Then the proud will suffer what has been set before them, finding their hands unable to do anything, as if they were being carried down in drowsiness. For you struck them with terror while defending your people and the places consecrated to you, so that the words fit: “A horse is a false hope for salvation”, and “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call on the name of the Lord our God; they were hobbled and fell, but we rose and stood upright” (Psalm 19:8-9 (20:7-8)) (Ps 20:8). The same thing as the hobbling and the fall is indicated here through the being carried down and the stupefaction.

Symmachus rendered it this way: “For the wrath of a human being will confess to you, a remnant of wrath girded on” (Ps 75:11). Since the wrathful and angry person who does everything in anger and not according to what is right is subject to confession and changes of mind concerning the sins he commits. For wrath is quick to lead to sin, bold even to the point of murder itself, so that the reasoning left behind in the soul after wrath brings strong repentances that wrap around the whole soul for what was wrongly done and said through wrath.

From the present psalm up to Psalm 82 (83), the discourse goes through the harsh and painful things concerning the people, and then in what follows it turns to brighter things (Ps 76 argument). In the present psalm he says that there is a long time in which the nation has been despised, sufficient to take away even the hope of help from God, unless someone remembers the former things and is strengthened in hope of the good things to come (Ps 76:2,3).

So indeed, having spoken piously in Psalm 72 (73), he now introduces the weak reasonings that come upon people in prolonged afflictions. And now he first gives thanks to God who received his supplications, describing his persistent prayer and the stretching out of his hands through whole nights.

When your power appeared, he says, everything was set in motion: the waters writhed in fear, and a turbulent struggle gripped the depths (Ps 76:17-19). Waters were also released from above out of the clouds, and the clouds ran through the sky with a great sound, and the arrows from heaven were hurled down. The sounds of thunder rolled around the circle of the sky as the clouds raced through, and lightning flashed across the inhabited world and shook the earth with an earthquake. These things point to the fearful wonders that appeared in Egypt, in the wilderness, and in Judea. For Egypt was struck with hail that came down with fire, and the waters of the Red Sea gave way as if shrinking back in fear. Thunder crashed in the sky and hail came down also upon the Canaanites in the war against the Jews. It is clear that lightning also flashed together with it. As for saying that the thunder sounded in a wheel, another passage says it was when he bound the axles of the chariots and brought them down into the sea with their commanders.

He presents to us the circle of the sky along which the stars revolve, like oxen going around a threshing floor (Ps 76:19). For a spherical heaven, according to the Greek account, is not to be found in the divine oracles, so that we should not imagine a wheel-like circuit above the earth and below the earth. For the divine Scriptures present water under the earth, not heaven, and waters above the heaven set as a boundary. For he says, “He stretches out the heaven like a curtain, he who roofs his upper chambers with waters” (Psalm 104:2). And the sun is said to run from one end to the other, from east to west, and not to run back from the west for even the smallest part of the day. And he says, “He established the heaven” (not “he who leads it around in a circle”) “and stretched it out like a tent to dwell in” (not “to be whirled around like a circle”). And Isaiah says that those who come from a far land come “from the end of the foundation of heaven”, so that the heaven is founded and standing, not running around in a circle. But these things are said for the sake of a brief reminder, so that we are not carried away to the fictions of the Greeks while neglecting the divine Scriptures.

He says that the divine way has no visible trace, unlike the human way. Therefore he called it a journey “in the sea and in the waters,” since Solomon says that not even the paths of a ship sailing the sea can be recognized, so that what is said is figurative (Ps 76:20-21). And it is no longer a journey of movement for God. For the Hebrews did not walk through the sea so that he might lead them through it, but the stretch of the Red Sea was brief for them in their journey, while the stretch through the land was long and lengthy. “You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (Psalm 76:21 (77:20)).

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 75 (76), explaining the psalm's imagery of mountains, the overthrow of the proud, and the contrast between trusting in horses and trusting in God.

title: God's hidden way made known in leading Israel, and the causes of his turning away
english: Yet even though your journey is invisible, this at least became known and clear to human beings: that you led the people on their journey out of Egypt as sheep led by Moses and Aaron. So the psalm gives this instruction ... in misfortunes ...

Others have explained these things this way. The psalm just mentioned ended in silence, neither searching out nor stating the reasons why the people were so despised by God their guardian. But this psalm indicates from the outset the cause of God's turning away, which God later declared through Isaiah when he said: "Is the Lord's hand not strong enough to save? Or has his ear grown too heavy to hear? No, your sins stand between you and God, and because of your sins he turned his face away from you so as not to show mercy" (Isaiah 59:1-2), and so on. So the psalm recalls Israel's disbelief and contradiction in the wilderness, in order to show that those who stand apart from God become the cause of their own evils, as David clearly narrates the events. And he begins at once in royal fashion, commanding his own people to attend to his law—or to his own instructions, as Symmachus renders it. For he says, "I offer the present exhortation as a kind of law."

And if, he says, God's love of humanity and pity and abundant propitiation had not preserved their succession, but he had pursued them with full wrath, they would have perished and become nameless. For God did not approve their choice, but had compassion on their weakness, as in the case of flesh that decays and spirit that departs.

The interpreters have given different accounts of this psalm's subject. One says the prophet simply laments a captivity and what happened to Jerusalem in it, without specifying which one. Another says it refers to the captivity under the Romans that took place after the betrayal of our Savior Jesus Christ. Others say it refers to the one under Antiochus, called Epiphanes. So let us set that question aside and examine some of the actual words.

The plea is against the nations, because they acted impiously and, being unclean, defiled the holy land and polluted the sacred temple. The appeal on behalf of Jerusalem is that the city once called holy to God has become a mound and a heap of stones—which Theodotion renders as "into a stone heap." These things can serve as a reminder of the election that had been made concerning Jerusalem. And he also speaks of the pitiable fate of its inhabitants: that even after death they were left unburied and exposed as food for birds, showing how great and savage was the enemies' treatment of the conquered. And he calls those who suffered these things God's servants, which carries a claim of kinship toward God and an appeal to the Master. For even if there are just charges against the servants, still there is a sparing of what belongs to him when it is inhumanly ravaged by an outsider. He also says that the bodies of the holy ones became food for wild beasts and that their blood was poured out without restraint like water before Jerusalem. Perhaps he calls the fallen "holy ones" because of their original election, just as the apostle also calls holy even the branches broken off for impiety, because they belonged to a holy root (Romans 11:16). Or perhaps he means that holy ones perished together with the unjust, which happens in the capture and destruction of a city and a nation, and which was shown through Ezekiel as happening. For he says: "Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against you, and I will draw my dagger from its sheath and destroy from among you"—Aquila says "righteous and impious"; the Septuagint, "and I will cut off from you righteous and impious" (Ezekiel 21:3-4). This had also been said more allegorically: "Behold, I kindle a fire in you, and it will consume every tree in you"—Aquila says "moist"; the Septuagint, "and every dry tree" (Ezekiel 20:47). The moist tree is an allegory for the righteous man, and the dry tree for the impious. The Lord himself showed that he is the true righteous tree when he said, "If they do these things when the wood is moist, what will happen when it is dry?" (Luke 23:31). And if the Lord shared in the misfortunes brought upon the world insofar as he shared in flesh, though he had no sin, it is no wonder that righteous human beings, who are in some way partakers of sin, also become partakers of the misfortunes that follow upon sins. They suffer equally with the unjust, being put to death just as he himself was counted among the lawless, yet they are distinguished before God. Such was the case of Jeremiah, taken captive among the ungodly, yet holding some distinction even among men after the captivity, in the honor he received from the one who took him captive.

title: The righteous share death with sinners but receive better things after death
english: But if a righteous man shares with sinners even to the point of death, then after death good things are already stored up for him, to mark him off from the wicked. This was the case with King Josiah. For indeed this man also, being most righteous, died in war while the Egyptian prevailed, because Israelite impiety had been great beforehand and did not receive pardon. So for the righteous themselves, if they suffer along with sinners, better things from God are stored up after the suffering (Ps 78:4). And for the brothers and kinsmen who suffer because of sins, there is great help through them, so that on account of their destruction some turning of God toward the nation comes about. This is also what the prophet now asks.

These words depend on a defense acceptable before God. For even if we deserve what we have suffered, he says, yet your name is reproached together with us, just as God himself says through Isaiah: "Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations" (Isaiah 52:5).
Because, he says, they ravaged the God-fearing nation like wild beasts and laid waste a holy land (Ps 78:7).

By naming the one who sits upon the cherubim, he reveals the heavenly authority through which all things are subject to him and nothing can resist him, if only he would appear. And he calls upon the power to be roused, because it has been silent and still and has looked on while the people suffered. Such were the things they suffered from the Assyrians; and he asks that the one who for the present is not with them, because of their abandonment, should come to them. But how would he come except in his working? For this reason he says, "Come to save us," as if he were saying, "Come by way of saving." And the words "Turn us and show your face" are because the one who has turned away from God cannot obtain the appearing unless he first turns back to him (Ps 119:36). For he says, "Turn to me, and I will turn to you" (Malachi 3:7). He asks this from the guidance and cooperation of God, as also in the words, "Incline my heart to your testimonies" (Psalm 118:36 (119:36)). For the pious attribute everything to God. And if your face appears, he says, we shall be saved; for the appearing of God is salvation (Ps 79:9).

The vine mentioned earlier covered the mountains with its shadow, because it surpassed every height and every power upon the earth, and with the spreading of its branches it covered the cedars of God, because it was supported by the divine powers and reached as far as the sea and the river. For this is also how the boundaries of the Judean land are named by God: "From the wilderness to the Euphrates, and from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines" (Exodus 23:31). Therefore the vine which you yourself, he says, brought out of Egypt and transplanted, which you made so conspicuous and extended so far—why did you look on while it was stripped of its protection and plundered by passersby?

Trumpets begin the winepresses according to the law. On the new moon of the seventh month he commanded a trumpet blast, and on the fifteenth day the feast of tabernacles. This was the gathering of fruits at the end of the year, in the collection of the works of the field, as is made clear in Exodus. And for the one who views the law spiritually, the trumpet blast would be a revelation of the trumpets that come from heaven, while the fast appointed for atonement on the tenth of the same month is a sign of that saying of the Lord: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (Matthew 5:4). For the law made the fast preparatory for the rest of the tabernacles and the joy in it, and by introducing beforehand the trumpets which signify the fear of the coming of the judge from heaven—since these announce beforehand the coming judgment, the humility for atonement follows, and so the feast for rest comes about. Let the psalm sung at the winepresses indeed correspond to the season of the feast according to the custom of the law, and for this reason let it mention trumpets at the beginning as a prelude to the feast of tabernacles. But let it signify the end about which it is sung, as the inscription reveals: when God gathers all fruits and gives the eternal tabernacles to his own. For in that end the good things are restored to those who are saved, and salvation from present evils—about which the previously mentioned psalms made their requests to God. [The rest follows in agreement with the preceding psalm.]

"Burdens," that is, the loads of lifting. For those who served in the labors of brickmaking carried the clay on their backs, throwing it out with a basket. So he removed their back, he says, from burdens—that is, he freed them from the loads (Ps 80:7).
